newsitem.title: BOTSWANA: Botswana says Lesotho leaders should reconcile.
newsitem.headline: Botswana says Lesotho leaders should reconcile.

text.p: Botswana's Foreign Minister Mompati Merafhe on Thursday appealed to Lesotho's leaders to cast aside their personal differences in the interest of the country.

"I hope that the principal actors in this very untidy situation will put Lesotho before their own personal interests and short-term ambitions," Merafhe told a news briefing on a forthcoming meeting of African Commonwealth countries to be held in Botswana next week.
"The country is going through turbulence at the moment but there is direct optimism that it will sort itself out," he said.
He said southern African countries were collectively trying to help restore mutual trust and confidence between the various players in the kingdom.

"The politics of Lesotho are at the moment very unclear, as they have been in the past. We in the region have done everything we could and will continue our efforts to help our friends in the region to rediscover themselves and ensure that democracy, good governance, accountability and transparency... become deep rooted in their culture," Merafhe said.
He said Botswana saw the Lesotho government as the legitimate government which had been democratically elected.

Southern African countries have been concerned at the threat against the kingdom's government by a group of rebel policemen who occupied the national police headquarters in the capital Maseru for 11 days from February 13.
The mutiny began when eight policemen refused to be arrested for the alleged killing of three fellow officers in 1995.
The army raided the police buildings at the weekend and arrested 100 officers including seven of the eight policemen.
The leader of the band Second Lieutenant Pakiso Molise is still on the run after he hid at the palace of King Letsie III.
The government, headed by the aging Prime Minister Ntsu Mokhehle, has questioned why the leader had been allowed to hide at the palace and has sparked further tensions between Mokhehle and the king.
Letsie, with the support of the army and police, dismissed Mokhehle and his cabinet in a royal coup in August 1994.
Mokehle, 78, was reinstated a month later after intervention by southern African leaders led by South Africa's Nelson Mandela.
